2024 · arXiv · Benchmarks & Evals

WorldSimBench: Towards Video Generation Models as World Simulators

A dual benchmark for video generation models positioned as "World Simulators": a trained Human Preference Evaluator scores generated videos on 20 embodied dimensions across three scenarios, while a separate closed-loop test converts the video into robot/vehicle/agent actions and runs it in a real simulator to see whether it actually works.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

The paper opens by sorting "predictive models" — anything that turns an observation plus an instruction into a prediction of what happens next — into a four-rung hierarchy by output modality: S0 models predict text (high-level plans), S1 models predict a single image (a goal frame), S2 models predict video (a plausible-looking future), and S3 models predict actionable video — video whose content is physically and geometrically consistent enough that it can be translated into real low-level control signals. The paper calls S3 models World Simulators, following the framing of Yang et al. (2023), and argues that no existing benchmark actually tests a model at that rung.

Its own survey of prior work (Table 1) makes the gap concrete: AgentBench, EgoPlan-Bench, MMWorld, and VAB all sit at S0 and score text output (task planning, multiple-choice, or an LLM/human judging text); LEGO sits at S1 and scores a single generated image by feature similarity; VBench and EvalCrafter sit at S2 and score generated video, but again by feature-similarity metrics against reference distributions — an aesthetic/fidelity judgment, not a physical-plausibility or actionability judgment. None of them can answer the question the paper is actually interested in: if you handed this generated video to a robot, a car, or a game agent as its next move, would it work? There is no ground-truth "correct" actionable video for an embodied task the way there's a ground-truth caption for an image, so a feature-similarity or reference-matching metric has nothing to compare against at S3 — which is precisely why the paper reaches for two indirect strategies instead: a trained human-preference judge, and literally executing the video's implied actions in a simulator.

// how it works

The method

WorldSimBench evaluates every model in three embodied scenarios chosen to stress different physical properties: Open-Ended Embodied Environment (OE), built on Minecraft gameplay video (the VPT / OpenAI Contractor Gameplay Dataset, Baker et al. 2022); Autonomous Driving (AD), built on nuScenes real-world driving data (Caesar et al. 2020); and Robot Manipulation (RM), built on RH20T-P robot-arm video with primitive-level instructions (Chen et al. 2024). Eight video generation models are put through the benchmark: Open-Sora-Plan(T2V), LaVie, ModelScope, OpenSora, AnimateDiff, DynamiCrafter, EasyAnimate, and a purpose-built Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V) variant — the authors modified Open-Sora-Plan's text-to-video model to additionally condition on a first frame, specifically to test whether image conditioning helps or hurts. Because the off-the-shelf open-source models produced low-quality embodied video on the target prompts, every model is first fine-tuned by the authors on scenario-specific data before being scored — the benchmark measures each model's fine-tuned ceiling on these scenarios, not its behavior fresh off the shelf.

Explicit Perceptual Evaluation

The first track scores a video the way a human would judge it, without touching a simulator. The authors define a Hierarchical Evaluation Dimension checklist split into three categories — Visual Quality (Aesthetics, Background/Foreground Consistency), Condition Consistency (Instruction Alignment, and, for OE, Scenario Alignment), and Embodiment (Trajectory plus scenario-specific dimensions: Velocity and Embodied Interaction for OE; Perspectivity, Key Element, and Safety for AD; Perspectivity and Embodied Interaction for RM) — giving 7 dimensions for OE, 6 for AD, and 7 for RM, 20 in total. Using GPT-expanded and human-verified prompts built from internet video captions, the authors generate a large pool of videos with the eight models and have humans score every video on every relevant dimension with a written reason, producing the HF-Embodied Dataset: 35,701 (video, instruction, multi-dimensional score, reason) tuples across the three scenarios (8,401 OE videos, 15,870 AD videos, 11,430 RM videos — the three subtotals sum exactly to 35,701). That dataset trains the Human Preference Evaluator (HPE): a LoRA fine-tune (only the LoRA parameters are trained) of the VideoLLM Flash-VStream, which takes a generated video, the generation instruction, and the dimension's textual definition, and outputs a score on a 1-to-n scale (n=2 for OE, since the paper treats OE quality as effectively binary; n=5 for AD and RM). Training runs 4 epochs at a learning rate of 2e-5 on 4 A100 GPUs; the human-written reasons are collected but explicitly not used as a chain-of-thought training signal, because "the reason labeled by different human varies a lot, hard for model to learn."

Implicit Manipulative Evaluation

The second track never asks a human or a judge model to look at the video at all. Instead, it treats the video generation model as the front end of a closed control loop: given the current observation and a text instruction, the model generates a short predicted video; a separately pre-trained video-to-action model (an inverse-dynamics or goal-based policy) converts that video into control signals; those signals are executed for a fixed number of timesteps in a real simulator; then the loop resamples a new predicted video from the current (now-changed) observation and repeats until the episode ends. Success is read directly off the simulator, not off the video. Each scenario gets its own simulator and policy: OE uses MineRL with a Steve-1-style goal-based policy (5 tasks — collect wood, collect dirt, collect seeds, explore/travel, dig — 10 trials each, capped at 3,000 frames); AD uses the CARLA simulator on the LangAuto-Tiny benchmark (routes under 150m) with an LMDrive-based policy, scored on the 8 standard CARLA-Leaderboard metrics; RM uses CALVIN with a Susie-based policy under CALVIN's standard train-on-ABC/test-on-D generalization protocol, run for 20 trials and scored on the percentage of chains that complete at least N of 5 consecutive tasks.

// what they found

The results

On the Explicit track's headline comparison — HPE vs. prompting GPT-4o as a judge, on the same videos, using accuracy (Acc) for OE's binary scale and Pearson correlation (PLCC) against human scores for AD/RM's 1-5 scale — the fine-tuned HPE beats GPT-4o in every one of the three scenarios: 89.4 vs. 72.8 Acc in OE, 0.60 vs. 0.28 PLCC in AD, and 0.43 vs. 0.07 PLCC in RM. Holding out one model's videos entirely during HPE training and validating zero-shot on it tells the same story for both held-out models: on OpenSora, HPE beats GPT-4o 71.6-to-66.5 (OE), 0.34-to-0.03 (AD), and 0.47-to-(-0.06) (RM); on LaVie, HPE wins 87.9-to-78.5 (OE), 0.49-to-(-0.04) (AD), and 0.44-to-0.17 (RM) — six wins out of six at the scenario-average level, with GPT-4o's correlation actually going negative twice (AD@LaVie: -0.04; RM@OpenSora: -0.06).

The Explicit Perceptual Evaluation of the 7 named models (Tables 7-9; the two Open-Sora-Plan variants are only both listed in the Implicit-OE table below) shows no single winner across scenarios: ModelScope leads OE (1.91 of 2), OpenSora leads AD (4.40 of 5), and DynamiCrafter leads RM (4.14 of 5). Two shared weak points recur: in OE, most models score poorly on Embodied Interaction (e.g. plausible object deformation like block-shattering); in RM, every model's Instruction Alignment score is low (1.0-2.6 of 5) while every model's Trajectory score is high (4.3-5.0) — the paper's own reading is that models move the arm smoothly but aimlessly, so the absence of a wrong, jerky trajectory inflates the Trajectory and Embodied Interaction scores even when the instruction itself goes unexecuted.

The Implicit Manipulative Evaluation surfaces a sharper, model-specific result. In OE, the paper directly compares Open-Sora-Plan's own two variants: the text-only Open-Sora-Plan(T2V) reaches an average task score of 26.38, while the image-conditioned Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V) — built specifically to add a first-frame condition — drops to 10.28, with its travel-distance score falling from 342.91 to 195.14; the paper describes the overall drop as evidence that "adding image input reduces its performance compared to the text-only condition," and reads the travel-distance drop specifically as suggesting "incorporating image data might interfere with certain tasks." The three purely image-conditioned models (Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V), DynamiCrafter, EasyAnimate) all score under 11 on this same AVG scale, well below every text-only model (13.10-27.80).

In the two closed-loop tests that require driving or manipulating a real simulator (AD and RM), only three of the eight models are actually reported — Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V), DynamiCrafter, and EasyAnimate. In AD, Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V) leads on Driving Score (31.054 vs. 24.491 for DynamiCrafter and 17.414 for EasyAnimate); EasyAnimate records zero Vehicle Collisions and zero Red Light Violations but by far the worst Layout Collisions (29.344, vs. 4.4-4.9 for the other two) — a metric where lower is better, so this is a weakness, not a hidden strength. In RM (CALVIN), DynamiCrafter completes the very first task in the chain most often (95% of trials) but its success rate falls off faster as the chain lengthens, so Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V) ends up with the best average completed chain length (2.95 of 5, vs. 2.75 for DynamiCrafter and 2.05 for EasyAnimate).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The dual-track design is the paper's real contribution, and it does something feature-similarity metrics (VBench, EvalCrafter) cannot: it makes "is this video physically plausible" falsifiable by actually acting on it. But a few things are worth separating from the headline framing.

The "across all scenarios" win is aggregate, not universal. At the scenario-average level HPE beats GPT-4o in all 3 finetuned comparisons and all 6 zero-shot comparisons in Table 3 — that part checks out cleanly. But the per-dimension breakdown (Table 6/Table 3's appendix twin) shows the zero-shot picture is messier than "HPE wins everywhere": in the OE zero-shot-on-OpenSora condition, GPT-4o actually scores higher than HPE on three of the seven dimensions — Instruction Alignment (80 vs. 60), Trajectory (100 vs. 22.2) and Embodied Interaction (88.8 vs. 80) — with HPE's overall win driven by big margins on Scenario Alignment (100 vs. 50) and Velocity (100 vs. 0.0). The paper's own text ("consistently surpasses ... across all scenarios") refers specifically to the finetuned, scenario-averaged comparison, and is accurate there — but a reader taking that sentence to mean HPE is uniformly better dimension-by-dimension in the harder zero-shot setting would be wrong.

The closed-loop "actionability" test — the paper's namesake claim — covers only 3 of 8 models in 2 of 3 scenarios. Every model gets the Explicit Perceptual Evaluation, and OE's Implicit test covers all 8 model/condition combinations because its goal-based policy can consume both text-only and image-conditioned video. But Tables 12 and 13 (AD and RM's closed-loop results) list only Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V), DynamiCrafter, and EasyAnimate — Fig. 5(b)/(c) label the tested entry explicitly as the TI2V variant, so LaVie, ModelScope, OpenSora, AnimateDiff, and the text-only Open-Sora-Plan(T2V) all never appear in a closed loop for driving or manipulation — five models in total. The paper's only stated reasoning is OE-scoped: Sec. 5.1 explains that the OE video-to-action model's goal-based policy "allows us to additionally evaluate text-to-video models" — which is why OE alone can score both conditions — but it never states the mirror-image restriction for AD/RM, never names which five models were dropped there, and never reports the gap as a scope limit (a plausible guess is that the AD/RM video-to-action policies need first-frame image conditioning that the excluded models don't natively support). Since "convert video into working actions" is the specific capability the S3/"World Simulator" label is meant to certify, the paper's flagship claim rests on a narrower evidence base — 3 models, 2 scenarios — than its 8-model Explicit sweep suggests.

Fine-tuning, not release quality, is what's being measured. The appendix states plainly, for all three scenarios, that "due to the low video quality produced by the open-source video generation model ... we applied additional fine-tuning using data from the [OE/AD/RM] simulation environment" before any evaluation happens. That is a transparent and reasonable design choice — these general-purpose video generators were never trained for embodied control — but it does mean every number on this page reflects each model's post-fine-tuning ceiling on WorldSimBench's own training data, not its zero-shot or released capability. A reader citing "OpenSora scores 4.40/5 on AD" as evidence about the publicly released OpenSora checkpoint would be over-claiming.

No inter-annotator agreement is reported for the human labels the entire benchmark rests on. The 35,701-tuple HF-Embodied Dataset is collected via "specific annotation guidelines and numerous in-context examples," with annotators told to score one dimension at a time in isolation — a sensible protocol — but the paper never reports how many annotators were used, what agreement (Cohen's kappa or similar) they reached, or any label quality-control step. Since HPE's entire claim to validity is "aligns with human perception," and GPT-4o is judged against the same human labels, the reliability of those labels is load-bearing and currently unverifiable from the paper.

The "first" framing is repeated at least six times, unhedged. "We take the (very) first step in evaluating World Simulators" (or equivalent) appears in the abstract, twice in the introduction, once in Related Work, once in the Conclusion, and once more in Figure 1's own caption ("We take the initial step in evaluating Predictive Generative Models up to the S3 stage") — none hedged with "to our knowledge" or similar. Table 1's own comparison shows this is at least well-supported (every prior benchmark it lists tops out at S2), but note that S3 is a category the paper itself defines, which makes a "first to evaluate it" claim close to definitionally true rather than an empirical finding to be checked against competing work.

baselines

Only one baseline evaluator is used throughout (GPT-4o prompted as a judge) — no comparison to feature-similarity/automatic video metrics (FVD, CLIP-score) as an alternative baseline, and no ablation of the VideoLLM backbone (Flash-VStream) HPE is built on.

contamination

Not a train/test leakage issue, but an adjacent one: every evaluated model is fine-tuned by the authors on scenario-specific data before it is scored at all, and the two tracks fine-tune on different data. The Explicit track's HF-Embodied Dataset videos come from models fine-tuned on VPT (OE), nuScenes with Vista-style sampling (AD), and RH20T-P (RM); the closed-loop tests instead fine-tune on VPT plus the authors' own collected videos (OE), the full CARLA/LMDrive training set (AD), and the full CALVIN(ABC-D) video dataset (RM) — only the OE source is shared between the two tracks. Either way, scores reflect adapted performance on in-distribution data rather than a model's native capability.

what's missed

The closed-loop ("does it actually work") evidence — the one thing no prior S0-S2 benchmark could offer — is present for only 3 of 8 models in AD and RM; five models (LaVie, ModelScope, OpenSora, AnimateDiff, and the text-only Open-Sora-Plan(T2V)) are never tested in a real driving or manipulation loop at all.

would raise confidence

Report inter-annotator agreement for the human labels; run the AD/RM closed-loop test on all 8 models (or state explicitly why 5 of them can't be); separate "fine-tuned ceiling" results from any off-the-shelf/zero-shot numbers if those exist.

// bottom line

WorldSimBench's dual-track idea — a trained preference judge plus an actual closed-loop actionability test — is a genuinely useful escape from feature-similarity video metrics, and the headline HPE-beats-GPT-4o numbers hold up under a row-by-row check. The framing to watch is scope: "World Simulator" evaluation is demonstrated end-to-end (video in, working control signals out) for a minority of the models tested, in a minority of the scenarios, on data the models were specifically adapted to.

// what to remember

What to remember

  1. WorldSimBench splits "is this a good world simulator" into two independently checkable tests — a trained Human Preference Evaluator (Explicit) and a closed control loop that converts generated video into real actions in a simulator (Implicit) — rather than the feature-similarity scoring VBench and EvalCrafter use.
  2. No model wins across the board: ModelScope tops OE, OpenSora tops AD, and DynamiCrafter tops RM on the Explicit Perceptual Evaluation, and every model shares the same Robot Manipulation blind spot — high Trajectory scores (4.3-5.0/5) paired with low Instruction Alignment (1.0-2.6/5), i.e. smooth motion that ignores the instruction.
  3. The paper's namesake closed-loop "actionability" claim is demonstrated for only 3 of the 8 evaluated models in the Autonomous Driving and Robot Manipulation scenarios (all 8 do appear in the Open-Ended Embodied Environment closed loop) — read the AD/RM headline numbers as evidence about Open-Sora-Plan(TI2V), DynamiCrafter, and EasyAnimate specifically, not about video generation models in general.
